Durban Plastic Spill [5129]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Production

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
State of Durban Beaches

On the 17th of October a huge storm hit Durban. Six people lost their lives and the damage to property is estimated to be about R98 million. Highways were flooded and a massive container ship the MSC Ines came off it’s moorings and blocked the harbour mouth.

The tug boats eventually managed to free it but as the tugs towed it towards its mooring, it once again broke free, due to strong wind, and was pushed into another ship, the Maersk Vallvick, that was already moored at D mooring on the point terminal. This caused some serious damage to the Vallvick which was crushed between the heavy container ship and the quayside. As the MSC Ines crashed into the Maersk Vallvick, the Vallvick’s accommodation area tore open and damaged a number of containers on the Ines, sending at least one severely ruptured container into the harbour.

On Wednesday last week, Jone Porter, the Director of uShaka Seaworld Education started noticing plastic pellets on the beach.

It caused a social media storm, reports from as far afield as Richard’s Bay rolled in of 100’s of millions of little round, half-moon shaped plastic “pellets” had begun washing up on beaches around Durban.
Within days it was evident that this was only the very tip of the iceberg and that the province’s marine life was under threat.
Towards the end of last week, SAAMBR (South African Association for Marine Biological Research) sent out an urgent appeal for all beach-goers to try and assist in collecting as many of these nurdles as possible over the weekend.
This call was echoed by numerous other organisations involved with marine conservation and beach clean-up projects.
According to SAAMBR, the pellets will very easily make their way into the food chain of many marine species, who could easily mistake the tiny pellets for eggs or similar food.
But that wasn’t the worst news. According to SAAMBR, the real danger is that these nurdles, which are a raw plastic material which gets re-melted and moulded in factories to make plastic products, can and do absorb pollutants like PCBs and organochlorine pesticides, which are highly toxic to marine life and humans if consumed.
Dr Deborah Robertson-Andersson who we interviewed for Microplastics’s students has done and experiment to show how quickly fish die when they eat toxic plastic.

Fundamentally, we have an enormous ecological disaster on our hands, which could easily be compared to an oil spill in terms of its possible impact on our marine species, not to mention the effects this could have on humans who may be consuming toxic fish a little further on down the road.

Transnet and the shipping companies have been silent. Had it been an oil spill more attention may have been focused on this area.

So are Durban Beaches ready for the holiday makers that will be descending to the beaches in droves.

South Africa was the first country outside Europe to be granted Blue Flag accreditation. 14 South African beaches lost their accreditation last year.Having a Blue Flag rated beach offers huge tourism benefits.
There are only two Blue Flag Beaches in Durban. While the plastic pollutants might not pose a threat at the moment, what about the quality of the water?

I have been in contact with several labs and the cheapest cost to do 10 water samples is R 2700. This will test E. coli and Faecal streptococci.
Beaches to test
1. Durban Main Beach North
2. Ushaka Beach (Blue Flag)
3. Blue Lagoon
4. Umhlanga beach (Previous Blue Flag)
5. Umhloti (Previous Blue Flag)
6. Westbrook ( Blue Flag)

We tested 5 beaches and only one Ushaka had abnormally high ecoli counts. I have been in touch with the municipality and asked them to do water samples when we interview them. They will also take us on an inspection of Durban beaches and facilities.

People to interview
1. June Porter – Ushaka
2. Dr Deborah Robertson Anderson – Marine Biologist
3. Refilwe (Student of Deborah)
4. Voxpops of volunteers
5. South African Marine Safety Authority
6. Ethekwini Blue Flag person

Nurdle Script

V/O
This is Durban soon to be the hottest place to be for over a 1 million holiday makers that will soak up the sun and surf.
With a turn over of nearly R6 billion a year tourism is crucial.
Having a beach with Blue Flag status is a draw card. Known for their excellent standards of safety, amenities and cleanliness, on the golden mile only Ushaka beach was awarded this accolade.

Ahead of the holiday season, we decided to test the water quality along 5 of KZN beaches for ecoli and faecal streptococcus.

“We dig into the 50cm quadrant and we allow the water to seep in and take a water sample.

V/O
On each beach UKZN marine biology students took 2 water samples.
They were all well within range except Blue Lagoon and Ushaka Durban’s only blue flag beach, which was about four times over the limit.

V/O
Dr Deborah Roberston-Andersson is a marine biologist at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.

“The bad news is that Ushaka and Blue Lagoon have levels over what would normally be considered safe for a Blue Flag Beach. For Blue Lagoon we kind of expected it as it is on the Umgeni River, but the reality is that Ushaka Beach was worse than Umgeni.”

Claire
“Why?”

Deborah
“Well Ushaka Beach if you think about it is right next to the Durban Harbour. The Harbour has 4 rivers that enter into it, so it has 4 times as much pollution as Blue Lagoon would have.”




V/O
We spoke to Durban Tourism about whether this would pose a health threat to the holiday makers.

Claire
“UKZN found high ecoli counts on Ushaka beach what would you say to that?”

Sbu
“We are aware that the results of the damage to our system is from the 10th of October floods, may have impacted on that.

V/O
Sbu Zondi is a Senior Manager of Communications at Durban Tourism.

“But we remain confident at Durban Tourism that come December our beaches will be ready.”

V/O
The recent storm Sbu is referring to, left a trail of death and destruction, with wave swells of up to 6m high.

Mkhize
“We were all caught by surprise by a severe storm that hit Durban and the surrounding areas.”

V/O
Captain Gqwetha Mkhize is the principal officer of SAMSA, the South African Maritime Safety Authority, and he says that in the 7 years that he has been working he has never seen a storm with such intensity.

Mkhize
“There were three similar size ships as this that had broken off their moorings and drifting off within the port

V/O
With the ferocity of the storm two ships collided with each other and three containers fell into the murky harbour waters.
It took 6 tugs boats to move one these ships that ran aground blocking the harbour entrance.

Mkhize
“Only one container was recovered on the second day, which was 11th at night now and it was really apparent that the container was heavily damaged and some of the cargo had spilled into the water.”

V/O
Although it was a freak accident unfortunately the containers carried tens of thousands of kilograms of plastic nurdles.

Link
“Nurdles are small pellets of plastic which serve as raw material in the manufacture of plastic products.”

V/O
The nurdles escaped from the harbour and due to their bouyancy were rapidly dispersing with the currents along the coast line.

Jone
“A couple of days after the very big storm, we started to see nurdles coming up onto the Ushaka Beach and the next day there were more and we realised that there was potentially a problem.”

V/O
Jone Porter from Usaka Sea World says that thousands of nurdles were deposited on the Blue Flag beach.

Jone
“There was a sense of urgency of getting the nurdles off the beach, we had no idea of the size of the problem.”

Link
The massive spill sparked a social media campaign hashtag show me your nurdles to create awareness and to encourage people to go out and collect nurdles on the beaches.

V/O
The problem was not just confined to Durban, hundreds of concerned citizens all along Kwa Zulu Natal’s coast line volunteered to collect the nurdles. Being light and tiny they are not easy to pick up.


Vox Pops
“It’s very hard to collect, it takes me about 3 hours to collect all of this stuff.”

V/O
There are reports of nurdles from Richards Bay to East London, it’s affected hundreds of kilometres of our coastline.

Claire
“Give us an idea of how much was lost?”

Mkhize
“When we recovered the containers, the total number of that was recovered was about 90 bags of 25 kg size out of 1900 bags that were in the containers.”

V/O
That means that 45 tons of nurdles were lost to sea, roughly around 2.275 billion nurdles.

Link
Nurdles pose no immediate danger to humans but when they enter the food chain that’s a different story.

V/O
Last year we produced an award winning programme on microplastics. Microplastics are small pieces of plastic that absorb pollutants from the sea with the result that they are up to a million times more toxic than the sea water.

V/O
“It’s estimated that by the year 2050 there will be more plastic in the sea, than marine life.”

V/O
Dr Roberston-Andersson has seen first hand the tragic impact of plastic. Part of her research work was in trying to rehabilitate baby loggerhead turtles.



Deborah
The juvenile turtles feed on blue bottles floating in the ocean and they were mistaking these very tiny pieces of blue plastic for blue bottles and no matter how we tried to rehabilitate the turtles the damage that had been done to the turtles was too severe and they ended up dying.


V/O
At UKZN Dr Roberston-Andersson says every animal they have studied recently has injested plastic.

V/O
Refilwe Mofokeng is a studying for her PHD in ecotoxicology and is researching how marine life absorbs toxic pollutants from plastics.

Claire
“How do animals in the ocean differentiate their food?”

Refilwe
“Most fish and animals are filter feeders so when you filter feed you just open your mouth and let everything in. But then most microplastics are whitish in colour which is similar to their food. They cant smell them because of that they get to be injested.”

V/O
Matthew Coote is a Masters student, his research is the first study to conclusively prove that the microplastics don’t just stay in the mullet’s gut but are absorbed into the tissue that is eaten by humans.

Matt
“So with a lot of the fish that get caught they get gutted, if you think you’re removing most of the plastics that way, they are actually still in the tissue so they are still being injested.”

V/O
It was the Mediterranean Shipping Company’s boat that lost the containers. The rule is the polluter pays and they have employed a local company to clean up the harbour and they have started cleaning up Durban’s beaches, after that they will move up the coast.



Sbu
“It is unfortunate that these are instances that go beyond what is controllable , as we call it a force of nature, but the city will be spending approximately 576 million in the cleaning up of the disaster of the floods.

However Cameron Johnston of Salt Fishing South Africa was one of the first facebook pages to break the story and he believes that not enough is being done.

Cameron
“We have municipalities from East London to Mocambique that need to have people on the floor and there is no contribution from municipalities or local government , this is an emergency as big as an oil spill because it isnt a massive black sludge on the beach we aren’t getting the same attention.”

Claire
“The area along the coast is vast is it possible to clean up all the nurdles.”

Hopewell
“I cannot for certain say it is not possible however the teams are working hard in assessing to fully comphrehend the magnitude of the situation.”

V/O
It seems an impossible task and many doubt that there is the capacity to tackle this problem.
The positive news is that the nurdle crisis has brought a huge amount of public attention to the scourge of plastics and Jone Porter encourages everyone to pick up not just the nurdles but any plastic pollution this festive season.

“For every cupfull that comes out that’s a few less animals that will be impacted.”

Promo 1 x 10 secs

A massive storm hit Durban recently, causing an ecological disaster, over 2 billion plastic nurdles are washing onto our beaches and threatening marine life.

Promo 2 x 15 secs

“This is a emergency as big as an oil spill, because there isn’t a massive black sludge on the beach we arent getting the same attention”

V/O
Over 2 billion plastic nurdles covering hundreds of kilometers of the KZN coastline is a catastrophic ecological disaster in the making.

Promo 3 x 15 secs

“In the past children used to pick up shells on the beach, but due to a huge spill in the Durban harbour, they are now picking up nurdles, what effects do these have on our environment.”

V/O
These plastic beads absorb pollutants that can have a toxic effect on marine life and the food chain.

Promo 4 x 15 secs

Hundred of thousands of holiday makers will be descending to Durban’s golden beaches. But a recent storm caused destruction and billions of tiny plastic pellets, called nurdles,have washed up on the shore. Can Durban authorities clean up the beaches in time?

There are only two Blue Flag Beaches in Durban. While the plastic pollutants might not pose a threat at the moment, what about the quality of the water? I have been in contact with several labs and the cheapest cost to do 10 water samples is R 2700. This will test E. coli and Faecal streptococci. Beaches to test 1. Durban Main Beach North 2. Ushaka Beach (Blue Flag) 3. Blue Lagoon 4. Umhlanga beach (Previous Blue Flag) 5. Umhloti (Previous Blue Flag) 6. Westbrook ( Blue Flag) We tested 5 beaches and only one Ushaka had abnormally high ecoli counts. I have been in touch with the municipality and asked them to do water samples when we interview them. They will also take us on an inspection of Durban beaches and facilities. People to interview 1. June Porter – Ushaka 2. Dr Deborah Robertson Anderson – Marine Biologist 3. Refilwe (Student of Deborah) 4. Voxpops of volunteers 5. South African Marine Safety Authority 6. Ethekwini Blue Flag person
